title: Compiler Front End: Lexing, Parsing and the AST
description: The first link in the parsing-to-executable chain. Write a lexer and a recursive-descent parser for a real language, produce an AST, and check every token and node against CPython's own tokenizer and parser plus a real specimen on disk.
author: Underlayer
completion_criteria: Read all 3 concepts, reproduce the 11-token stream and 9-node AST of courses/front/assets/samples/specimen.src with runner/frontier.py, and drive the interactive runner until your parser and the independent oracle agree on a source you typed. The runner never evaluates your expression and never executes your input.

concepts.title: A Lexer You Can Check
concepts.description: MEASURED. A lexer turns characters into named tokens; this one skips whitespace, emits NUMBER, NAME and OP pairs, and refuses an unexpected character with its zero-based offset. The specimen produces 11 tokens, checked against CPython 3.12.2's tokenize module rather than asserted. Bounded input: 4096 characters.

concepts.title: Recursive Descent, Written Out
concepts.description: MEASURED. Four functions -- expr, term, unary and primary -- turn the 11 tokens into 9 AST nodes. The precedence hierarchy is the operator-precedence table of the Python Language Reference read 2026-11-28, and left-associativity is the while loop inside each level. A leading minus builds a USub node, not a negative literal: the Language Reference says negative numbers are unary operations, and ast.parse proves the shape.

concepts.title: The Tree, and a Runner You Can Disagree With
concepts.description: MEASURED. The specimen tree has 9 nodes and root Add(a, Div(Mult(2, Sub(b, 3)), 4)), identical to ast.parse after conversion to the course's node encoding. The interactive runner takes learner-authored source, tokenises and parses it with the lesson's code path, and compares the resulting tree BY VALUE with an independent Pratt parser -- and with the shipped fixture when the source is the specimen. No eval, no network, no file access, 4096-character input bound and a 100000-step parser budget.

exercise_decls.question: What does the lexer emit for a space between two tokens?
exercise_decls.answer: nothing — a NUMBER and an OP are adjacent
exercise_decls.options: nothing — a NUMBER and an OP are adjacent|a SPACE token|one merged NUMBER
exercise_decls.explanation: Whitespace is skipped before any token is produced, so grammar rules never have to mention spaces.
exercise_decls.hint1: Re-read the unit about the finger moving across the text.
exercise_decls.source_quote: nothing — a NUMBER and an OP are adjacent

exercise_decls.question: Complete this sentence from the lesson: The specimen is ______, followed by one newline.
exercise_decls.explanation: The lesson states: The specimen is a + 2 * (b - 3) / 4, followed by one newline.
exercise_decls.hint1: Find the sentence in the reality unit and read the highlighted term.

exercise_decls.question: Why is the multiplication function called before the addition function in the grammar?
exercise_decls.answer: because * and / bind tighter than + and -
exercise_decls.options: because * and / bind tighter than + and -|because * appears earlier in the specimen|because multiplication is faster to compute
exercise_decls.explanation: A tighter-binding operator must become the child of the looser one, so the function for it is one level deeper in the call chain.
exercise_decls.source_quote: because * and / bind tighter than + and -

exercise_decls.question: Complete this sentence from the lesson: negative numbers such as ______ are syntactically not literals.
exercise_decls.explanation: The lesson states that negative numbers such as -3 are syntactically not literals, but unary operations involving the minus operator.
exercise_decls.hint1: Find the quoted Language Reference sentence in the reality unit.

exercise_decls.question: What does the runner do when your tree and the oracle tree differ?
exercise_decls.options: prints DISAGREE and both trees|prints the arithmetic answer|hides the result
exercise_decls.explanation: It reports DISAGREE and prints both canonical trees, so you can find the first decision that diverged.

limitations: The language is integers, names, +, -, *, / and parentheses only; no floats, exponentiation, strings, calls, statements or error recovery beyond a first-error message.
No runtime values are computed: the specimen is parsed, never evaluated, and no claim about a or b is made.
The oracle is specifically CPython 3.12.2 on Windows; other Python versions and implementations were not checked.
This is the first link only: semantic analysis, type checking, IR, code generation, object files, linking and loading are deliberately deferred and are not taught here.

The browser runner compares two parsers inside one page; it does not execute learner-authored program code, and the Python sandbox runner is a constrained exercise envelope, not a security-grade isolation boundary.
